extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, research mathematicians, and scholars interested in mathematical practice and proof epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing mathematical proofs for their epistemic contribution beyond mere theorem-truth — i.e., judging proofs by the methods, concepts, connections, and network effects they carry. Useful for philosophers of mathematics, journal editors, referees, and mathematicians deciding when a proof is a substantive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof convey reusable approaches or strategies?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav lists 'strategies and methods' as a key thing a proof carries: reusable approaches that other mathematicians can apply to different problems. A proof that teaches a method scores highly here; a one-off trick scores poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof reveal links between definitions and other theorems (clarify conceptual relationships)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs should make explicit how concepts relate and fit into existing theory. Rav emphasizes that conceptual relationships help situate the result and make its content intelligible and usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof surface heuristic moves or patterns that succeeded on this problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristics are the practical moves and problem-solving patterns a proof exhibits; these are valuable for attacking similar problems and for pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions clarified
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof show why the chosen definitions are appropriate or clarify definitions used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav stresses that a good proof can vindicate or refine definitions, showing which aspects are essential and which are artefacts of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-results worth their own attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof produce lemmas or intermediate results that are independently interesting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extractable lemmas increase the proof's value because they can be reused elsewhere; proofs that produce such sub-results contribute more to the discipline's toolkit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples ruled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof implicitly or explicitly rule out plausible counterexamples, thereby delimiting the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof that identifies boundary cases or excludes counterexamples conveys information about the theorem's scope and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof indicate directions in which the result extends (suggest generalizations)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that suggest how hypotheses can be weakened or conclusions strengthened point to future work and increase applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof explain why certain hypotheses are needed (clarify restrictions)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good proofs show the role of hypotheses; they explain which parts of assumptions are essential and which may be artefacts of the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to other proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof embed the result in the literature by linking to other proofs and bodies of work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav values proofs that place a result within a web of existing arguments, helping to 'triangulate' and corroborate it via multiple perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof exemplify a particular proof-type or methodological tradition useful for future reference?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying the kind of proof (e.g., combinatorial, geometric, analytic) provides a precedent that guides later proofs and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof establish the theorem's truth (provide a truth-warrant)? (necessary but not sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav acknowledges that establishing correctness is necessary. However, truth-warrant alone is minimal; further knowledge-content criteria determine the proof's substantive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-content
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof teach a strategy or method useful beyond this theorem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Rav's multi-functional rubric: method-content evaluates whether the proof transfers know-how—procedural knowledge about how to approach similar problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-content
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof clarify or refine the relevant concepts (concept-content)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to 'definitions clarified' — measures whether the proof improves conceptual understanding or suggests conceptually better formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection-content
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof create links to other parts of mathematics (connection-content)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axis assesses how the proof strengthens ties across areas, making the theorem part of a broader network of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic-content
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof teach generalizable heuristics (heuristic-content)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the extent to which the proof trains readers in problem-solving attitudes or strategies that can be applied elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization-suggestiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof indicate where and how the result might be generalized?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 'generalization paths': looks for explicit hints or structural features that suggest broader contexts for the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction-clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof make clear what limits the result (restriction-clarity)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether the proof identifies which assumptions are essential and where the theorem fails or needs modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network-density (systemic cohesiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof strengthen the network of mathematical knowledge by linking results and providing triangulation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav's systemic-cohesiveness idea: reliability and value partly come from a proof's contribution to the tightly woven network (more connections, triangulation, and identification of weaknesses increase value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel proof content / contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Does a new or alternative proof contribute distinct knowledge (new methods, connections, or perspectives)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why multiple proofs of the same theorem can be valuable: a new proof that is shorter, more explanatory, more general, purer, or differently styled provides separate epistemic contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the proof shorter or simpler, thereby simplifying the area?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter proofs can make the subject more accessible and reduce reliance on complicated machinery; simplicity is a form of explanatory virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof increase understanding by explaining why the theorem is true (explanatory proof)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory proofs are valued for making dependencies and reasons transparent (Rav notes 'more explanatory proof' as a desirable feature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof achieve greater generality (apply in broader contexts)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more general proof extends applicability and shows deeper structural reasons for the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof exhibit 'purity' (clarifying what the theorem really depends on)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Detlefsen-Arana and Rav, a purer proof isolates the essential ideas and avoids extraneous machinery, thus clarifying dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different-style/approach value
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof employ a different style (e.g., geometric vs algebraic), connecting the result to other communities or perspectives?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different styles can reveal distinct conceptual frameworks and make the result meaningful in other subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: one-off trick (poor proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof rely on a one-off trick that yields no transferable knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav marks proofs that merely verify a conclusion with an ad hoc trick as poor: they add little to mathematical knowledge because they do not transfer methods or concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: opacity about methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the proof opaque about its methods (fails to communicate its strategy)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opaque proofs hinder understanding and reuse; good proofs make their methods explicit and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: hiding connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proof hide or fail to disclose connections to known results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that obscure links to the literature reduce systemic cohesiveness and fail to triangulate the result within the network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: non-robustness to variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the proof brittle (cannot be modified to handle slight variants)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust proofs suggest generalizable methods; brittle proofs that collapse under minor changes are less informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization insufficiency / knowledge beyond formal derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the informal proof carry epistemic content not captured by a mere formal derivation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav criticizes the formalist view: even if an informal proof can be formalized, the informal version often carries methods, heuristics, and conceptual relations that formal derivations do not preserve. Evaluation should therefore measure knowledge-content beyond formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion for AI-generated proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does an AI-produced proof deliver extractable methods, strategies, or conceptual insights in addition to correctness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rav's framework implies that formally verified AI proofs that only establish theorem-truth but provide no transferable knowledge should not be considered full contributions to mathematical knowledge. Evaluation rubrics for machine proofs must include metrics for knowledge content, not just truth-warrant.
